sentences.text: Every vaccine in the world is named after a cow.
So how did a cow end up inside the most important medicine ever made?
By the end of this film, you'll know how a milkmaid's hand, a country doctor and one careful test turned an old farmyard rumour into the medicine that wiped a disease off the face of the Earth.
In the seventeen-hundreds, the most feared disease in the world was smallpox.
People called it the speckled monster.
It caught kings and farm workers alike, and about three in every ten people who caught it died.
Many who lived were scarred for life, and some were left blind.
Picture yourself in an English village in those years.
When smallpox arrived, you would see a neighbour's house shut up and silent, hear the church bell toll day after day, and wonder whose house would be next.
Parents counted their children only after they had survived it.
There was one way to fight back, and it was risky.
Doctors took a little matter from a smallpox sore and scratched it into a healthy person's arm.
It usually gave a milder illness, and lifelong protection.
It was called variolation.
But some people died from it, and they could pass full smallpox on to others.
So people faced a terrible choice.
Risk the treatment, or wait for the monster to come.
If it were your child, which would you choose?
In the countryside, though, farmers had noticed something strange.
Cows sometimes caught a disease of their own, called cowpox.
It made small blisters on their udders.
And the milkmaids who milked them sometimes caught it too, on their hands.
It was a mild illness.
A few sore spots, a day or two of feeling unwell, and that was all.
But in the dairy country, people said something odd.
Anyone who had had cowpox would never catch smallpox.
Imagine being a milkmaid in a smallpox year.
While your neighbours lock their doors, you walk to market without fear, because you had a few sore spots on your hands from the cows.
It sounds like an old wives' tale.
But it kept coming true.
Some farmers even acted on it.
In seventeen seventy-four, a Dorset farmer called Benjamin Jesty scratched cowpox into the arms of his wife and his two sons, to protect them.
It worked, but he told almost no one, and he never wrote it down for doctors to read.
Not far away, in the little town of Berkeley, a country doctor called Edward Jenner had heard the same story from his patients.
Jenner was a curious man.
He studied cuckoos and hedgehogs, sent up one of the first hydrogen balloons ever seen in England, and wrote poems for his friends.
But the milkmaids' story was the puzzle he could not leave alone.
As a boy, Jenner had been put through variolation himself.
He knew how hard it was.
His old teacher in London, the surgeon John Hunter, had once given him some famous advice.
Why think?
Why not try the experiment?
So Jenner started collecting cases, of people who had caught cowpox and then never caught smallpox.
For years, he wrote them down.
But a list of stories isn't proof.
Jenner needed a test.

parts.chapter_card: A Pail, a Lancet and a Boy

sentences.text: In May seventeen ninety-six, a young dairymaid called Sarah Nelmes came to Jenner with cowpox on her hand.
She had caught it from a cow on a nearby farm.
A cow later remembered by the name Blossom.
Jenner saw his chance.
On the fourteenth of May, he took a little matter from one of the spots on Sarah's hand, and placed it in two small scratches on the arm of a boy called James Phipps.
In his own notes, Jenner described him simply as a healthy boy, about eight years old.
Over the next week, James felt a little unwell.
A slight fever, a poor appetite, a night of restlessness.
Then, just as Jenner had hoped, he was perfectly well again.
Picture Jenner in those days, watching the boy run about the garden.
If the old saying was wrong, he had given a child a disease for nothing.
If it was right, he might be holding the key to the most feared illness on Earth.
So James had caught cowpox.
Now came the question that really mattered.
Would it protect him from smallpox?
On the first of July, Jenner did the test.
He gave James a standard variolation, the old treatment that used real smallpox matter, which would normally cause at least a mild illness.
Then he waited.
One day.
Three days.
A week.
Nothing happened.
In Jenner's words, no disease followed.
Months later, he tried again.
Still nothing.
The cowpox had protected the boy.
Jenner wasn't the first to try cowpox.
Benjamin Jesty had done it twenty-two years earlier.
What Jenner did that was new was test it, carefully, and then publish every case, so any doctor could check his work and do it themselves.
He tested more people, and in seventeen ninety-eight he paid to print a short book.
He called the disease by a Latin name, variolae vaccinae, which means smallpox of the cow.
From vacca, the Latin word for cow, came the name for the treatment: vaccination.
Not everyone believed him.
Some doctors mocked the idea, and cartoonists drew people sprouting little cow's heads after their jab.
But the results were hard to argue with.
Jenner sent cowpox matter to anyone who asked, and in a little hut in his own garden in Berkeley he vaccinated poor families for free.
Within a few years, doctors were vaccinating people across Britain, Europe and the Americas.
A lifetime later, the French scientist Louis Pasteur made new treatments that trained the body to fight other diseases.
In honour of Jenner's cowpox, he proposed calling them all by the same name.
Vaccines.
So every vaccine, for every disease, still carries the name of a cow.
And Jenner's idea went further than he could have dreamed.
In the twentieth century, health workers travelled to every country where smallpox still lived, vaccinating everyone around each new case, until there was nowhere left for it to go.
On the eighth of May, nineteen eighty, the world's health leaders declared that smallpox was gone.
A disease that had killed hundreds of millions of people over the centuries had been wiped out, the first ever ended by humans.
Why was this so groundbreaking?
Because it showed that the body can learn to fight a disease before it ever meets it.
A mild, safe cousin of an illness can teach your body to recognise the real thing.
That one idea is behind every vaccine you have ever had.
And because no one alive today needs a vaccine against smallpox, most of us have never seen it at all.
The speckled monster is something you will only ever meet in a history book.
A milkmaid's hand, a country doctor, and a boy who stayed well.
Together, they turned a farmyard rumour into proof, and gave a cow's name to medicine.
Long before Jenner, another mystery frightened people every summer.
To solve it, a printer in Philadelphia flew a kite into a thunderstorm.
